utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, we understand you haven't been well but that you're prepared to go on. If, at any stage, you want an adjournment, ask for it and of course you can have it if you're not well. You're not obliged to go on. We'll keep the session -- since we're a bit late starting, we'll keep the sessions fairly short for you to cross-examine the witness, but beforehand Ms. Bauer has a point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, overnight we made available the patches that were outstanding that need to be tendered. There are three patches. The first one is premarked 349, tab 18, a Serb Chetnik Movement patch, and I would like to offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: The next patch is a specialised police patch and is pre-numbered 349, tab 19. And the third patch is pre-numbered 349, tab 20. It's the Falcons from Toput, Lopare in BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Erstic, you explained that you were arrested at the beginning of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spent a total of one month there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many of you were there in that prison?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 120 altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Altogether?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that you were in the old building at the Knin hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that building had been turned into a prison, or was it used for something else?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a prison and there were some soldiers there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big is the building?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can I tell you? You could put 300 people in it maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You're a mason. You know the proportions of buildings. You're a builder and can assess that.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have time to count how many rooms there were to the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's a very small building in actual fact. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, medium sized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many rooms did you all take up? When you say "you," I mean all the people that were detained there, in how many rooms?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were about 15 rooms as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people in your room with you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you were exchanged, that was a month later?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the International Red Cross attended, did it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the treatment you received in the month that you spent in prison like?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean towards us?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. How did they behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't be able to know -- only people who were there could know what that treatment was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, so tell me.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were beaten. We were mistreated. They forced us to do various things. They didn't allow us to sleep. The food was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had to load up ammunition and weapons and unload flour, things like that. We had to dig canals, load up coal in Knin and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the working hours you would be taken out of the building of the old hospital to perform some physical labour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how big were these groups?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, how large were the groups of people taken off to do these work assignments?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes six, sometimes eight, ten, four. Depending on the requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did anybody receive any injuries from the beatings and so on?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were injured, but nobody dared say they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And when you came under the auspices of the International Red Cross, were you able to tell them of your injuries and all the things you experienced over there, all the problems?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could, but we didn't dare do so because they told us beforehand that if anybody complained to the International Red Cross about what was going on, that you were being mistreated and beaten, you'll be really beaten up. So we didn't dare say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Erstic. But you were taken for an exchange; right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Afterwards we were exchanged, and when we were exchanged we could say what happened to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But while you were in prison, how many times did the International Red Cross come to visit you when you said you didn't dare complain to them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what intervals?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some -- every ten or 12 days roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during that month that you were incarcerated in the prison there, you weren't without International Red Cross supervision for longer than an a ten or 12-day period; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If not more than ten or 12 days expired without the Red Cross visiting you, then I assume that if you were beaten, the representatives of the International Red Cross could notice the traces of those beatings on you.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't see because those who were badly beaten up were shut up in other rooms so that the International Red Cross had no idea about these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that the International Red Cross didn't have permission to tour all the premises, all the rooms in this hospital building which, as we know, wasn't a big one?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They weren't allowed to visit all the rooms because there were special rooms for these seriously injured people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that every ten or 12 days you would meet these representatives of the International Red Cross and you claim that you were injured. Could they notice those injuries on you, on your person?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, when they bust up your ribs, nobody can notice that because you're covered in clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, when you were exchanged -- once they exchanged you, and I heard you say something along those lines to Ms. Bauer, that you were exchanged -- a hundred of you were exchanged for 60 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Twenty people from Lika remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in prison.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, once you had been exchanged, those 100 of you for those 60 Serbs, where had those Serbs been before they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, once you were exchanged, did you then explain to the International Red Cross, after that month or so that you spent in prison, that is, did you explain to them what had happened that you had been mistreated, and did you show them your injuries then, and bruises? And did you talk to them at all about things like that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't ask us much, just brief questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you tell them when they asked you these brief questions?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were mistreated, that the food was bad, that we'd been beaten, that we were forced to do labour assignments, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any reports or minutes or notes taken by the International Red Cross recording the fact that you had been mistreated and beaten?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if they made notes of what we told them. They just asked us that in sort of a formal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean you -- they weren't interested in it, actually, they just asked you as a matter of course?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they ask each individual?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not each individual, but in passing maybe us 130, but we heard it all. Well, they asked what the treatment was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I said earlier on, that we were mistreated. We were beaten every day, every night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any doctors on that Red Cross team, International Red Cross team?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you examined after you had been released? When did a doctor examine you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day, straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where? Where were you examined?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zadar and in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, do you have any documents to bear that out about the injuries you sustained?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they started making requests for pensions and things like that, I went to the doctor in Zadar and asked him to issue those papers, but he said that it all happened during the war and that the papers are lost. And I have an uncle in Rijeka, so I went to Rijeka. And he said, "Well, we didn't register that. We didn't record anything in any log-books or anything like that," so they had nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had no documents although you were there for a month and your injuries must have been visible? You have no medical certificate to bear that out?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right, I haven't. I just went to see the doctor, he gave me some medicines, I took the medicines he gave me, and that's it. Afterwards I wasn't able to get a single piece of paper from the doctors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the people who were incarcerated with you in the prison have any medical certificates of any kind or documents which would indicate the injuries they sustained there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Some people do have documents like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me who, for example. Give me a few names.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was that man, Mikulic. He was from my village but he was arrested later on. You mean during the time I was incarcerated there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Of the hundred that were exchanged, the ones that you know about. Can you give me a few names?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. I didn't see them around afterwards once I'd left myself, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know whether any of them have any medical documents?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we didn't see each other after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this, please: You did your military service in the JNA in Serbia in 1987 to 1988 in Zemun - did you not? - the barracks there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, while you were in Serbia, did you have any problems whatsoever due to the fact that you yourself were a Croat?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so -- on one occasion I actually did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, describe the problem you had.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was transferred to Kragujevac, I was on a factory farm there owned by the army, and there were just about 15 of us there, and we looked after the pigs and the calves and so on. We worked on the land. We would sow corn, wheat and so on, those kinds of things. And a month or two later, I can't tell you exactly but I think it was around about October, there was a sergeant there and he was very good towards me, but when the harvest came, he said, "Erstic," this one officer actually, "Erstic, you're going to answer me. I'm going to ask you something." And I said, "Yes, sir, warrant officer, if I can." And he said, "Of course you can. You'll know the answer." And then this is what he asked me, "Tell me, what you are by way of ethnicity, nationality, are you a Serb or a Croat?" And I said I was a Croat. He didn't answer, didn't say anything to that, just turned round and left. And then I saluted him in passing, I would -- that was my duty, but he never uttered a word to me after that, and I left the JNA. I think his name was Petar Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only unpleasant incident was that you were asked what your ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he refused to talk to me after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that during that time in the JNA there were Croats and Muslims and Albanians and Macedonians, Montenegrins, Slovenes, all the different nationalities? So how do you explain this? He didn't say anything to you. He didn't make any comment. He just asked you that question.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me that question and turned around and left and never addressed me after that. Whereas beforehand, before that, he would even make some jokes and we would have some fun together, laughs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that, you concluded that he assumed a negative attitude towards you, is that it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I found it a little strange. After having asked me that he never said a word to me. I would say hello to him, salute him but he didn't respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that seems a bit strange for me too, so it's difficult for me to believe that but anyway, let's move on. You say the Croats and the Serbs got on well together up until about 1988 or 1989. That's what you say, when Milosevic started to make his speeches. Those are your words.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, which speech of mine did you hear in which something was said that might have been against the Croats or against any people in Yugoslavia? Which speech did you hear?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I watched you on television yourself when you were holding those rallies in Belgrade, when you were shouting, "We want a Greater Serbia, and all Serbs have to live in one state."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erstic, you could never have heard that on television from me to say that we want a Greater Serbia and that all Serbs have to live in one state. And you claim -- you could never have seen that and then you claim that you saw that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you must be the only person who saw it.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not alone. Plenty of others saw it too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that rally when you heard me say that we want a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Belgrade, sometime in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were my words, you say?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that that is what you claim. Did someone tell you that or are you claiming that you yourself saw that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that myself with my own eyes on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then I won't ask you anything more about that, because I assume you know that there are recordings of all those speeches. Tapes are available. And you actually claim I said, "We want a Greater Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's very good. Now, tell me, please, in 1990 you became a member of the HDZ. I see that from your statement.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the HDZ, according to the principles of its programme, already in February 1990 advocated an independent Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I see on page 2 that as a member of the HDZ, you welcomed the referendum for Croatia's independence.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I voted for the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on the basis of your own knowledge and experience at the time, what can you tell us? Was there a Croatian problem in Yugoslavia, the problem of Croatia? Did it exist in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a problem as soon as these slogans of a Greater Serbia started to be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you hear those slogans?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the HDZ was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And where did you hear such slogans being made?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started on television; where else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw reports on Greater Serbia even before the HDZ was formed, on television?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you celebrated after the referendum.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also say that in Croatia, everyone was happy except for the Serbs, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They celebrated their own, and we celebrated ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you celebrated after the referendum. Everyone was happy except the Serbs. Why were the Serbs not happy? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say they were not happy. They were happy because they already suspected what would happen. They were even happier than we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. They were even happier than you when that referendum was held on the independence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That is not what I meant. As soon as you had stated that there would be a Greater Serbia and that all Serbs would live in one state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, that is what made them happy. I see.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that I never said that.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can claim that you didn't. Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that why the Serbs were not happy was because certain rights had been abolished for them in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Serbs didn't have rights in Croatia, then I don't know where anyone in the world had any rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know that their status that they had had according to the Croatian constitution had been abolished?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know anything at all regarding what was done towards the Serbs in those days, for instance, in 1990, 1991? When were you in prison? You were in prison in 1991, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything done in 1990 or 1991 towards the Serbs because they might have been disturbed?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that Serbs, during those years, were advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Serbs were not really for preserving Yugoslavia. They wanted Yugoslavia to fall apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. That is what you know.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you know that, how do you explain the fact that at those elections at which the HDZ won, that is a fact, that is not my allegation, most Serbs voted for the League of Communists of Croatia, the SDP led by Ivica Racan, and not for the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is not true that they had voted for Ivica Racan. They voted for the democratic Serbian party, because wherever you turned, there were posters to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not talking about posters of all the parties taking part in the elections. What I am asking you is that most Serbs in Croatia then voted for the League of Communists of Croatia and not for the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the anti-Serb campaign launched after these elections and the victory of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I really was not involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, at least you could have seen it in the Croatian press. I'm not talking about the press in Belgrade because you didn't live there, but in the Croatian press in the course of 1990, could you see anything about the incidents involving Serbs? Do you remember the incident when that Ustasha sign was written, the letter U on the Serbian religious parish in Bogoviceva Street in Zagreb? This was in March.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you quite frankly, I don't read the press much now and I didn't before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember when the formation started of the volunteer youth units in Croatia and various events which caused a great deal of nervousness and fear among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was at home. I was tilling the land, looking after the cattle so that I didn't interfere with those things much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember the name Tjelesni Zdrug or the Croatian National Guards or the Sokol guards or volunteer youth units of Civil Defence of Croatia? So I've quoted four different names of these organisations. Do you remember when those formations were formed at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I won't ask you anything more about that. Tell me, do you remember that, because you say that the Serbs hated the Croatian flag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So their reaction was negative to the Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the chequerboard flag, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that this chequerboard flag was the symbol of the independent state of Croatia during the Second World War when many Serbs were killed in Croatia, when they were the victims of genocide?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Second World War was a long time ago. You're asking me too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think that 50 years later a symbol of crimes in the Second World War --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. The witness can't help us about this, and we've been through it with a large number of other witnesses anyway. So let's move on to something which he can deal with, connected probably with his village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him, Mr. May, in view of the fact that he said that the Serbs had a negative attitude or, as he put it, hated the Croatian flag, to explain to me if he knows the reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need to go into it with this witness. It's a matter we've dealt with a great many times already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the attack on Krusevo in the summer of 1991 was a turning point?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was this attack on Krusevo in 1991 a turning point when you know very well what preceded the summer of 1991, the events in Croatia that preceded it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why the attack? Because the Greater Serbia had already been launched. It was arming the Serbs in Croatia, and upon assignment, they went from one village to another to destroy everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is your explanation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the Serbs had automatic rifles as you say manufactured in the Crvena Zastava factory in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that that was the only factory manufacturing those weapons, that is the automatic rifle in Yugoslavia? It was the weapons envisaged by establishment for the whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know, because I too was issued the same rifle in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those rifles existed in the JNA and the Territorial Defence in all the republics throughout Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the Territorial Defence, and all that went into Serb hands. It was distributed to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about who got hold of them, because probably they were not the only ones, but you say that they had rifles manufactured in Serbia. So everyone had rifles manufactured in Serbia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these people that you refer to in your statement, the armed men in Krajina? Were they the people you knew from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some while I were there. There were some I knew. There was others I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you mean there were people who were not from your village.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know all the people in Knin and in the environs?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the locals, and in Knin there were people from Serbia and from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you see from Serbia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Captain Dragan's soldiers, and judging by their accents when we made their beds. And we washed the premises, and we washed the windows and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I gathered from Captain Dragan's statement that he went there alone and he engaged in the training of local military conscripts. He didn't bring anyone with him. He came all the way from Australia.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they spoke real Serbian, because I spent a year in Serbia and know how Serbs speak, how Croats speak, and how Bosnians speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, when you're describing your arrest, is it true that you were not arrested by the JNA or any unit from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. It was the local Serbs, the soldiers of Milan Martic or the police, Milan Martic's police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not Milan Martic's police. It was the police of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of Krajina. And he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the men who held you in detention were members of that police, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that among the detainees there were members of the National Guards Corps who were captured in the fighting in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of the National Guards Corps were there that were captured during those battles?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20 or so of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, since you say all of you who were in detention were Croats, were you absolutely all Croats or were there also some Serbs who were imprisoned there or people of other nationalities? Because people can be sent to prison for various reasons?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were only Croats, from Dalmatia, actually. No one else was in the prison. From Dalmatia and Lika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all of these then exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the people from Lika stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know were they later exchanged as well?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the principle known then that there were exchanges all for all?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied to Dalmatia, all for all. And the last thing that happened was that Gospic and Knin had to negotiate with their own people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were dealt with separately. You say 100 Croats were exchanged for 60 Serbs. If it was an all-for-all exchange, all of them were supposed to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That applied to Dalmatia, 100 Croats, and the rest were different from Gospic and Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So somebody was waiting for the other side from Gospic and Knin to release Serb prisoners according to the all-for-all principle?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, since you were arrested only in October 1991, and you stayed in prison until November 1991, how many Croats remained living in Knin, continued living normally without any problem?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a big question. How could I possibly know how many Croats remained in Knin?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you know anyone because you lived in the vicinity, and probably as a mason you must have worked in Knin at some point. Did you know the Croats who lived there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single one, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know a single person?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I rarely went to Knin. And I wasn't really interested in who was Croat and who was Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anyone at all in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Knin itself? Well, I knew one man who lived -- who drove a bus in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to speed this up. You said that you had seen General Mladic in uniform, although you were not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he or any other JNA soldier had nothing to do with your arrest?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That much is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he had something to do with your release, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he did, because he was in charge there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Namely it was he who organised, together with Martic, that you be released from prison and taken for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your statement that Captain Dragan's men came to see you, gave you cigarettes and treated you decently.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't come to see us. They asked the guards who were guarding us to get us to come to their quarters to make their beds, scour the floors, clean their lavatories, and they treated us decently. I have to say that much. It's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they help you in any way?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, at that time it was quite enough for us that nobody beat us while we were in their quarters. They gave us cigarettes. They treated us like normal people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the escorts of this delegation of the ICRC, was there a Croatian representative, Ivo Covic?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He introduced himself and said that he was from Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He stretched out his hand for a handshake. It was very brief. Just an introduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to tell him at least, if not the foreigners from the ICRC a couple of words about the conditions you were living in, how you were faring there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. When he asked us we had to say it was fine, because we knew what we were in for if we said anything else. So we had to lie and say that everything was all right, lest we be beaten and mistreated later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at one point were you taken to a JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were all released from that prison and put on a bus, the buses left and we didn't even know where we were going. We knew nothing at all. And then we arrived at a barracks. We could see that it was a barracks. There were soldiers around in olive-green/grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that tell you that the army was taking you over and that they were taking you to your release?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had said dozens of times that, "Your exchange would happen tomorrow or the day after tomorrow," and it never happen before, and so we didn't really trust them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could they have promised you 50 times that it would happen any day now and you had lost hope, whereas you spent a month in prison only?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would tell us the same thing in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. It was a form of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was a form mistreatment, promises of exchange?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They kept talking about it and it never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, from the day you were brought to the prison to the day you left there was only a month?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1993, you were in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were involved in the Storm operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in that Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened. Well, the Serbs had fled. We liberated the place. We came back to our homes. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know anything at all about the suffering of Serb civilians in that Operation Storm? Because you participated in it. As a participant, you must have some idea.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any Serbs either alive or dead or wounded. So my conscience can be clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What unit were you in?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Home guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did that unit go then?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the area of Velebit, Mount Velebit, Golubici, some village there. Others had come there before us, and we followed in. We came by truck, and since we were able to get in by truck, it means there was no longer any danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't go any further. You just stayed where you were brought.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they brought us there and unloaded us there, and we spent there one day and one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see a single person dead, alive, or wounded, and you know nothing about how many people got killed in that operation?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything at that time when you were already in the Croatian army about Croatian prisons holding Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But this thing in the Operation Storm, the people who stayed behind, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in anything you know about it.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were those centres where civilians were placed, elderly people. I believe there was one in Zadar, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about anything else about the one in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as you know, how were they treated?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either because I didn't go there to see them. I was not in charge of that, so I can't tell whether the treatment was good or bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea about the camps instituted for Serbs in your immediate vicinity such as the town of Biograd Na Moru, not to speak of Virovitica, Glina, Vrginmost? Did you know anything about those camps?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the events in Gospic, which is also in your immediate vicinity, about the camps that existed there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know? I know nothing about that. Gospic is far away from me. I've never been there in my whole life and I'm 35 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after the Operation Storm did you remain with the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We demobilised about a couple of days later, maybe five or six or eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went back to your village after that and you were no longer involved in those formations again?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that whole operation you didn't fire a single round and you were not involved in any military action?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody shot at me and I didn't shoot at anyone and I had an easy time of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know nothing about what happened?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Erstic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No re-examination either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Erstic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Since the witness is no longer with us and when a witness is here I want to raise other matters, you said we were late because I was feeling unwell. The only thing I had asked for was a pain-killer, and that's all. Otherwise, as you know, I never complain about anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. Very well. We will have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Ivan Marjanovic, and he testifies also without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Ivan Marjanovic, declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, you have already stated your name. On the 18th June 1993, did you review the statement given to an investigator on the 2nd of March, 1991, and confirm its accuracy in a legal proceeding?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender the 92 bis statement as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 511, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will read now briefly the main points from this statement. Mr. Marjanovic, a Croat farmer aged 63 at the time of the events lived in Nova Krslja, a small settlement of 18 Croatian homes in a predominantly Serb-inhabited area of the Slunj municipality. It is in the region close to Rakovica, Kordunski Ljeskovac, and Drecnik Grad and Your Honours, it's such a small place and also the village of Lipovaca that it is not actually in the atlas, but you find the other three villages on page 20 in grid 4B, and just below the division line between grid 4B, 3B and 4B, just for your orientation. The village Lipovaca which was close to the village of the witness is about three times bigger than this Nova Krslja. Relations were harmonious between the two ethnic groups until the elections in Croatia in 1990. Beginning of 1991, the police split along ethnic lines and barricades were set up in the region that made movement very difficult. The witness, therefore, stayed in the village throughout the relevant time period. On the 27th of October, 1991, Serb soldiers led by Milan Popovic came to the village and arrested all young Croat men they could find including the witness's son Marijan. Popovic introduced himself to the witness as the commander of the police unit of the JNA in Zeljava. Zeljava was close to Bihac and was a military airport. Popovic wore a standard JNA uniform with the cap with the five pointed star. Some of the soldiers that were with him were local Serbs and they wore black police uniforms. The soldiers searched the witness's house for weapons. Mr. Marjanovic, I have one question in relation to the soldiers that came to your house. Among the soldiers that wore the regular JNA uniform, were there any -- any soldiers who seemed to be conscripts from other regions in the former Yugoslavia, and if so, from which region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that, that they were from --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they spoke Macedonian amongst themselves, and that was just a little way up from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. The young Croats were taken to the military prison at Zeljava where they were held and beaten continuously. Fifteen days later, the witness's son was released. He was bruised all over his body. On the 28th of October, 1991, Serb soldiers returned and -- to the house of the witness and demanded that he surrender his rifle although the witness did not have any rifle. The soldiers then beat him severely. They also hit him with a cable which broke the witness's arm and wrist. The next day, soldiers came again and told him that he was not allowed to leave the house or the immediate surrounding of the house. A couple of days later, Nedjo Kotur came to the witness's house and told him that the Serbs had killed some Croats, and he told the witness to go with him to bury them. Kotur was a local Serb, a local Serb commander, and he was dressed in a JNA uniform of a reserve officer, and he wore a JNA hat with a Red Star. Together with Kotur and three other Croat villagers, the witness drove to Lipovaca. On the drive, when they passed the checkpoint manned by Martic men, Kotur changed his JNA hat against a black beret. A bit further down the road he again put on his JNA hat. They all went to the house of Mate Brozincevic in the village of Lipovaca. In the kitchen they found the body of Mate Brozincevic having several bullets in his stomach. The witness also saw that Mate's wife, Rosa, had been shot and the son's body, the son Mirko, was lying on his side in the entrance of the bedroom and he was shot through the neck. The witness and the other Croat villagers buried the bodies in front of the house. Then they moved to the house of Franjo Brozincevic. They saw the bodies of Franjo Brozincevic, his wife Mira, and the daughter and mother, Marija Cindric and Kata Cindric, the latter a very old lady. They were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. lying on the floor, and all these people had been shot and the witness and the other Croat villagers buried them also in front of the house. When -- during your -- the preparation for your testimony, sir, did you review a list of names of victims in Lipovaca, and did you add additional information, in particular their ages?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did review it, and I know all of them in order, all the men and women who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also know their ages and did you add these information --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time -- what was it you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also tell the -- me, tell me the anxious of the -- the approximate ages of the victims?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have actually prepared a list of the additional information that we got from the witness during the proofing and would like to tender it as an additional exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You actually should have it. It's tab 2. Sorry. It's tab 2 of this little bundle that you got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'm -- I'm against admitting part of an indictment as evidence, using the indictment as evidence. Is this not an annex of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we have actually exhibited these annexes already, and all the witness did is add the approximate age of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it is enough to know that this is Annex I, paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, when you came to Lipovaca on that day, did you see any destruction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I saw some destroyed houses, actually houses that had been burnt, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Croatian villagers from Lipovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When these people were buried, that was when I saw two men who were there, who were who were fairly near, Smolcic Nele, and he brought me some planks and nails and the things we needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to these two men afterwards?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the reasons. They were there and I know nothing about them after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? Are they missing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They're missing. They -- their families after Operation Storm came to look for them but nobody knew what had happened to them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 13 of your statement, you described how you were ordered to go to the military command in Kordunski Ljeskovac on the 4th of August, 1995, and we do not need to repeat that. But when you returned to your village, did you find your family and the other villagers still there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't find my family, but I found the other villagers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your family?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My family had left and gone to Ruma. They ordered my son Marijan to switch the engines on to his tractor and trailer and to take the rest of the family to Ruma also. They were also Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ordered him? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Nova Krslja, Ilija Kovacevic, one of his sons, who worked for the police, ordered them and Rade too, a man called Rade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Serbs that were on the trailer. How many Serbs did your son transport?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Serbs that were on the trailer, and my question is: How many Serbs did your son transport?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 40 with all the luggage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they told?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: And they said the Mujahedin were coming from Bosnia and would slaughter everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I just noted that this is not just the annex of the indictment. The witness put some annotation on that. So I think it's quite admissible. So I suggest the Chamber to admit it. You can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That is actually what I meant. The additional points that the witness knew about the victims. Your Honour, this concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Examine for about ten minutes and then we'll take the break. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, in your municipality or, rather, in your village of Nova Krslja, it's not a municipality, it's a village I assume.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understand it, in 1991 there were about 300 houses to the village; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And only 18 were owned by Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you didn't take -- that you were liberated by Operation Storm and that about 35 people were killed or, rather, bodies exhumed of people who were killed by the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on what grounds do you say that they were killed by the Serbs? And do you have any information as to how those people lost their lives in fact?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: All the people who remained in the village were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in your village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from -- not my village but Drecnik Grad, Saborski, Ilinovac those places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you visit those places, the ones you just told us of, at any time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know all those places, but all those casualties were taken to Drecnik Grad when the exhumation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you learnt about it just when the exhumation was taking place, is that it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how do you explain this claim that they were killed by the Serbs if in fact you first learnt about all this once the exhumation had started?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness does not claim in his statement that these 35 people were killed by Serbs. He only testified that he heard about the people from Lipovaca, that seven victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which -- which paragraph deals with the 35, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's paragraph 14. And that's just the mentioning of the victims, not who -- how they were killed and who did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The statement says: "I aware that there were others killed in the area because I know there were about 35 people exhumed from graves in surrounding villages." Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we're on point 14, as Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said a moment ago, in order to save time I am going to take advantage of this to read out paragraph 14. You say that during the war,: "I did not lose a single member of my family, and nobody from my village fell victim."

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There you have a full stop. And then you go on to say: "I know that some other people from our region were killed because I know that in the surrounding villages 35 bodies were exhumed." So what I wanted was to ask you this: In view of the fact that none of your family members and nobody from your village was killed, so on the one hand that is what you claim, and I assume it's the truth, and we've already noted that in Nova Krslja there were 300 houses of which only 18 were Croatian houses, which means that it was a predominantly Serb-inhabited village and not a single Croat of those villagers there in your village was killed during the whole war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me then, please, today, after the Operation Storm, how many Serbs are living in those 300 houses which existed before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They've all moved out and left for Serbia. Now, at present, there are only four houses. And all the rest -- actually, the rest are coming back and their houses are being built up again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean eight years after Operation Storm, there are only four houses or households; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say in your statement that up until 1991, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, there weren't any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to say, and this is all in paragraph 2 of your statement, or point 2, whichever you like, that you came to realise that the Serbs wanted to create a Serb Krajina and that my speeches introduced discord among the population. That's what you say. You say: "I heard several of Milosevic's speeches being delivered," and I will skip this because you say the speeches of other politicians too, "and I came to realise that the speeches were entering -- that were leading to discord among the people." So what speech was it of mine that you thought led to discord?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain this to me? I'm not quite sure. What do you mean my conversation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I always heard you talking and at all the rallies and all the talks and conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What talks and conversations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you were talking. When you were saying something where -- in some places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, give me an example, because the previous witness also mentioned my speeches. What is it that I said that introduced discord amongst the Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that you were establishing a Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, did you hear that with your very own ears? Did you hear me that we were setting up a Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did hear it several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, do you know that I never said that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard it nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what you say you heard. You say you heard me allegedly say things like that. Was that the only reason that there were tensions among the Serb inhabitants of your region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems which the Serbs at that time had in Croatia in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs didn't talk to the Croats much after that, but I have good neighbours who saved me a number of times during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But your village is the best example because there were only 18 houses and not a hair of their head was harmed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Just two houses were burnt, and those houses were burnt because there were Croatian policemen inside. So just two houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Marjanovic. Now, you say that in 1991, you saw some local Serbs carrying rifles.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me why were they arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't arming them. You know best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any attacks against the Serbs before they started arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- you have your headset on, so I assume you can hear me properly. Were there any attacks on the Serbs before the Serbs started arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't feel any attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you didn't move around outside your village anywhere, did you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no problems there, were there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't move around anywhere, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in that same paragraph, you go on to say: "I knew that a Croatian referendum was being organised, but I was afraid to go and vote because it was too dangerous as I lived surrounded by Serbs."

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody threaten you, any of your villagers in that village of yours?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nobody harmed you at all? Nobody threatened you or did anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said that tensions were growing when she gave us the background to your testimony, she said that barricades had been set up.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of paragraph 2, you say in the last sentence: "I never saw any barricades, but I heard that there were some in Petrova Gora, Vojnic, Korenica, Slunj, the lakes of Plitvice and so on."

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as far as other people have testified, there were barricades, but all I want to establish is that you yourself never saw any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. barricades, did you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that had no effect on relations or tensions in your village, did it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say in connection with having seen local Serbs with rifles that you realised that they were making problems and that the police had become separated into the Serb police and Croat police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know that this separation or division occurred because -- precisely because of Croatia's state policy?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a politician. I never had anything to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I respect that. Now, do you know why there was this separation and divide in the police force?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you ever hear that -- about the constitutional amendments in July 1990 adopted by the Croatian parliament or Sabor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I wasn't listening to any news of that kind at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm sure is you'll remember those days when the symbols, the coat of arms with the chequerboard motif on it and the symbols of the same Independent State of Croatia were revived of the state during World War II? You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they established that the only official script to be used would be the Latin script. You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you say that the police split up into two groups, do you know that in Croatia at that time it was from the internal affairs department or rather from the police force a lot of Serbs were dismissed as well as unreliable Croats? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Serb refugees, ever since October 1991, in fact, moved out of Croatia in great waves? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: And so did the Croats. They went to Zagreb too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Serb refugees as far as back as October 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, then, do you remember any pressure that was brought to bear by the Croatian forces and the Croatian state and the Croatian authorities at that time against the Serbs for which the Serbs left, the Serb refugees left the area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did any news reach you? Did you watch television, read the newspapers or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't read the newspapers then, and I don't read them now. All I have to do is to make ends meet. That is what my life is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Marjanovic, but if we bear in mind the fact that you lived in a village in which as you yourself say nothing happened, there was not a single casualty, you didn't read the newspapers --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. No Serbs fell casualty in my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And neither did a Croat, I assume.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, neither did a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yet you spent the entire time there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what are you testifying about here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm testifying about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: About what happened. You've heard what he's testifying about. He's testifying about the bodies in the village. Do you want to ask him about them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do. But, Mr. May, I've already asked him whether he knows anything at all about how those people came to lose their lives, and as far as I understand it, the witness's answer was that he knows nothing about that, that the first information that reached him about all that was when they were brought for burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what year was that? When were those corpses brought? After Operation Storm, was it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means at the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was at the end of 1995 when the bodies were brought over there.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to bury them and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1995, after Storm. One or two months after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. One or two months after Operation Storm. So that would place it in September or October?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the parents came and the family members. They came to see me to ask me whether I knew anything and the police, the Croatian police also came to see me and I told them that I went to bury the bodies, and they said, "When the exhumation is to take place, we'll come and fetch you," and they came to fetch me and then I told them who I had buried where, and everybody was taken to the Drecnik church and cemetery, and that's where these people were finally buried, in that large cemetery there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your village before the war, was there any Territorial Defence organisation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the surrounding parts, were these -- ZNG organisations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Drecnik, Rakovica, Draganac, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Drecnik, Rakovica and Draganac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those are precisely the places in which you said there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was no shooting in your village and they weren't there in your village, were they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Afterwards, the Yugoslav People's Army shot from there at Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the Yugoslav People's Army shoot at Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 1991 to -- right by my house, there were cannons and all that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that period of time when you saw members of the JNA and those cannons by your house?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
